evidence.claim: Rail transport helped connect the towns along this corridor: service reached Riverton from Manassas in 1854 and soon extended to Strasburg.
evidence.quote: Rail service was established in 1854 with the construction of the Alexandria, Orange and Manassas Gap Railroad between Manassas and Riverton. This line was soon extended to Strasburg

evidence.claim: Strasburg’s pottery factory later became a railway depot, then a museum in 1970.
evidence.quote: The building was once home to the Strasburg Stone and Earthenware Manufacturing Company and later was converted to a Southern Railway depot. It operated in this manner until the early 1960s. In 1970, it opened as a museum.

evidence.claim: Strasburg’s nickname, Pot Town, came from making both everyday and decorative earthenware and stoneware.
evidence.quote: Later nicknamed “Pot Town,” Strasburg also became a center for the production of both utilitarian and fancy earthenware and stoneware pottery.

evidence.claim: One factory building traces what happened next: built in 1891 for the Strasburg Stone and Earthenware Manufacturing Company, it changed to railroad use in 1913.

evidence.claim: The two-story brick structure served as a Southern Railroad station and depot before the Strasburg Museum opened there in 1970.
evidence.quote:
The building served as a station and depot for the Southern Railroad.
The Strasburg Museum opened in the building in 1970.

evidence.claim: Its displays include local pottery alongside railroad artifacts and a model railroad, bringing those successive uses together in one building.

evidence.claim: Signal Knob’s view into the northern Shenandoah Valley made it a military observation point during the Civil War.
evidence.quote: From Signal Knob, the Confederate Signal Corps could monitor Union troop movements and observe battles from Winchester to Fisher's Hill and beyond.

evidence.claim: Both Union and Confederate armies used the peak; Confederate signalmen occupied it from 1862 to 1864 and communicated with other stations using flags, lanterns and telescopes.
evidence.quote: Signal Knob was used by Signal Corps in the American Civil War by both the Union and Confederate armies.  The Confederates occupied it from 1862 to 1864.

evidence.claim: In October 1864, John Brown Gordon studied Union positions at Cedar Creek from here before devising a surprise attack.
evidence.quote: In October, 1864, Confederate Major General John Brown Gordon surveyed the Union position at Cedar Creek from Signal Knob and devised a plan for a surprise attack.

evidence.claim: The attack succeeded that morning, but a Union counterattack defeated the Confederates later the same day.
evidence.quote: The Confederates successfully carried out the attack the morning of October 19, 1864 at the Battle of Cedar Creek, only to be defeated later that day by a Union counterattack.

evidence.claim: The Massanutten Trail leads to the peak, where Civil War fortification remains survive.
evidence.quote: The Massanutten Trail, maintained by the Potomac Appalachian Trail Club, leads hikers and mountain bikers up to Signal Knob.
